On that date the board's inspectors rejected 73 boxes containing 42,785 pounds of rib backs on the ground of slime, odour and some mould.
Now 42,785 pounds is a lot of meat, particu- ' larly when you can scarcely get a pound of bacon in Canada. I would ask the minister what final disposition was made of that meat. He knows that when we cure our own bacon on the farm we often have a struggle with a little mould on the outside. I should like to know whether this meat was salvaged, and whether we have since eaten it, in addition to the other types of meat I have discussed.

Any meat which is condemned is sent back to the plant that produced it to be reconditioned before being put on the market again, or it may be used for tankage or some other purpose.
I have been asked, Mr. Chairman, that the committee rise at twenty minutes to six, which is five minutes from now, and therefore I shall not attempt to make a speech at this moment.
I would suggest to the committee that we have been discussing the marketing service and agriculture on two different amendments which were moved to the address, and also on a motion to go into supply and on two amendments to that motion. In other words, we have had weeks of discussion of these items and have now spent the greater part of to-day on them. I would suggest that, after I have answered as shortly as I can one or two questions that have just been asked, the

Supply-Agriculture
committee might allow the marketing items to pass so that at the next sitting we can discuss the special items.
Replying to my hon. friend's questions, we certainly could not retain the British market in competition with Denmark and other countries if we followed the suggestion that has been made of sending our poorer bacon to Britain and retaining the good product at home.	k
So far as beef is concerned, we have been sending praactically all our canner cattle overseas in cans. Last year we sent 126,000,000 pounds of canned meat to Britain, and it was the poorer pork and the poorer beef that was put into those cans. That is always the case in our canning processes here in Canada. It must be remembered, however, that we are in competition with the Argentine in canned meat and the Argentine follows quite a different practice. They put very good meat into cans, and if we want to compete with them in that trade we shall have to do differently from what we have been doing. The greater part of the 400,000 odd head of cattle which have been shipped out of this country in the form of meat during recent years has been the poorer beef. As a matter of fact, under the arrangements we have we are not permitted to send more than twenty per cent of our red and blue beef out of Canada. That is provided by the prices board regulations. We have never got up to that twenty per cent. Only a very small percentage of our red and blue beef, which is the highest quality of beef we have has gone out of this country for export. We are eating it at home. I know from experience in my own home that in the last three or four years I have been eating the best beef that I ever ate in Canada. When the United States market was open we sent our best beef to that country, but that market is now closed and we are consuming the greater part of our red and blue beef at home.
The other question had to do with the 90 per cent. I never at any time said that we were marketing 90 per cent of our A's and B's in Britain except for two months last fall. Hon. Ben Smith telephoned me one morning to ask if we could not supply Britain with more bacon. I told him over the telephone that we would try to do so, and during a two months' period we raised the amount going to Britain to 90 per cent of our A's and B's. Ordinarily we send from 70 to 85 per cent to Britain, but during that two months' period we sent 90 per cent.
What percentage of the meat is being consumed in Canada?

I could not state the exact percentage offhand, but if my hon. friend will put the question on the order paper I will answer it. The figure can be got, but first I would want his definition of poorer meat.
Can we hope that a greater proportion of good bacon will be released for consumption in Canada?

It is not a question of whether any more ,can be released. It is a question of whether we can market the quantity we desire to market and thus retain our marketing position. If we turned all the good bacon that is produced in Canada on to the home market, the price, irrespective of anything that this government might do, would not remain high very long.

I do not want to be discourteous to the Chair or to the minister, but I have been waiting for this item to ask a question about hog graders that I asked at a previous sitting, when the minister asked me to wait until this item was before the committee. How many hog graders have you in the Dominion of Canada and how, do they work? Do you keep them in one place the whole time or change them around like the cream graders-leave them in a plant for three months? How long do you keep them in a plant at a time? When the committee meets again will the minister tell us what are the duties of a stockyard agent?

The answer to the first question is, about seventy-five. The answer to the second is that they rotate, in a community like Winnipeg, for example, from plant to plant, and not always for the same length of time. It depends on the plant and on the individual; sometimes it is a week and sometimes it is a month.
Would the minister give me an answer some other time as to how long they stay? I think it is far longer than a month.
If the hon. member will write me a letter indicating what he wants to know, I will reply to it.
Certainly. And the minister will tell me what a stockyard agent is?
Call the next item and let us carry that.
